<meta>continues from previous page: the entry under the heading "Moistened Stems and Soaked Leaves." Author attributions in the poem section run together with the verses in the manuscript, and several names are uncertain readings.</meta>The <term>Xijing Zaji</term> <gloss>Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital</gloss> says: Dong Zhongshu said, "In times of great peace, the rain does not break up the clods of earth; it only moistens the stems and soaks the leaves, and that is all." <note>Dong Zhongshu was a Han dynasty Confucian scholar. Gentle rain that nourishes without damage was seen as a sign of good government.</note>

Poems

Then fine rain is made to gather a light chill; I sit and listen to it pattering against the window paper. <note>The manuscript writes a character resembling "pity" where "window" is expected.</note>

It hurries the gulls early; the spring catkins drift without strength, scattered over a crumbling wall.

The clouds are heavy, the sky hangs low, and the rain goes on and on; fine drops float in before anyone notices, and the water spreads faint ripples across the whole pond. *Shi Ping* <note>attribution uncertain</note>

At midnight, in the pond pavilions of the Five Marquises, a beauty wakes with a start, grieving for the flowers. <note>The "Five Marquises" stands for powerful noble families. The following characters may be a further author's name.</note>

It dyes the mountains a thousandfold green and washes away the dust until all six directions are clear. *Du Guangting* <note>a Daoist master and writer of the late Tang and Former Shu</note>

A wild wind, like a hand, uproots withered trees; leaping waves, like thunder, split the bridge apart. *Xin Yuzong* <note>attribution uncertain</note>

Little by little the willows darken the road I came by; slowly clouds rise over the mountains I gaze toward. *Du Ziráo* <note>attribution uncertain</note>

Rain startles the fish from the bait, and the old angler heads home, fishing rod in hand, stepping down from the mossy rock. His home is by the ferry landing, so he pushes on through the wet; the scattered sound of dense drops chases after his straw raincoat. *Ding Hui*

At midnight I think back on the affairs of ten years past; all at once, with the rain, they come into my heart. *Du Kehe*

I try to write a poem of joy at rain in a time of peace: On the eastern upland the earth is newly broken and the plough sinks deep. It has already relieved the anxious toil of the emperor of ten thousand chariots, and should ease the minds of the Three Dukes who harmonize the order of the world. <note>The Three Dukes were the highest ministers, charged with keeping Yin and Yang in balance.</note> Heaven seizes the unruly dragon and whips it till it bleeds; thunder drives the harmonious energy to pour forth as rain. The farmers on the ridges idly discuss its worth: an inch of sweet moisture is worth an inch of gold. *Shi Jie* <note>a Northern Song Confucian scholar</note>

Long afflicted by the sun of Zhao Dun, I rejoice to meet the rain of Fu Yue. <note>Zhao Dun's harshness was likened to the summer sun in the Zuo Zhuan. Fu Yue was the minister of the Shang king Wu Ding, who was told to be like "a timely rain" for the people.</note> *Su Shi*

<summary>This page completes a Han-dynasty saying about gentle rain in times of peace and then gathers poetic couplets on rain by Tang and Song authors, including Du Guangting, Shi Jie, and Su Shi. The verses praise rain as a blessing for farmers and a sign of good government.</summary>
<keywords>rain, poetry anthology, Dong Zhongshu, Xijing Zaji, Du Guangting, Shi Jie, Su Shi, Fu Yue, Zhao Dun, agriculture, good government, leishu</keywords>

The Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital <note>original: 西京雜記</note> states that Dong Zhongshu <note>a prominent Han dynasty scholar</note> said: In times of Great Peace, the rain does not break the soil clods; it merely moistens them with a gentle dew.

### Poetry

Let the fine rain bring a light chill once more; I sit and listen to the rustling sound as it strikes the window paper. It urges the gulls along in early spring, while the willow catkins fly feebly, sprinkling the crumbling walls. The clouds are heavy and the sky is low as the rain falls continuously; fine droplets drift down unnoticed by men. Tiny ripples rise and fill the pond.

At midnight, within the pavilions of the Five Marquises, the beauties are startled awake, grieving for the flowers. The mist dyes the purple mountains a thousand-fold emerald; it washes away all dust, leaving the six realms <note>the universe: North, South, East, West, Heaven, and Earth</note> pure. 

Du Guangting writes: The wild wind is like a hand uprooting withered trees; the surging waves are like thunder splitting broken bridges.

Xin Yu writes: Looking back at the path where the willows grew dark, clouds gradually rise over the mountains in the distance. 

Du Zirao writes: The rain startles the fish as they feed, and the old fisherman returns, holding his fishing rod as he descends the mossy bank. His home is at the ferry crossing; he departs through the dampness, the splashing sound of many droplets following his straw raincoat.

Ding Hui writes: In the middle of the night, I think of things from ten years ago; in an instant, they all come to my heart along with the rain.

Du Kehe writes: Written to celebrate the rain of a peaceful era. It has just broken through the eastern fields to the depth of the plow; it has already relieved the Emperor's <note>literally "ten thousand chariots"</note> anxious worries and should satisfy the hearts of the Three Dukes <note>high ranking officials</note> who harmonize the world. Heaven seizes the mischievous dragon and whips it until it bleeds; the thunder drives the harmonious energy, venting it as mist. On the ridges, farmers leisurely discuss the value: every inch of sweet rain is worth an inch of gold.

Shi Jie writes: Long have we suffered under the scorching sun <note>metaphorically "Zhao Dun," a historical figure associated with the summer sun</note>; now we joyfully encounter the seasonal rains <note>metaphorically "Fu Yue," a legendary minister who brought rain</note>.

Su Shi <unclear>not transcribed</unclear>

<keywords>rain, poetry, Great Peace, Dong Zhongshu, Du Guangting, agriculture, metaphors for governance</keywords>

Can a stroke <note>original: 中風, Wind-stroke</note> also present with a tight pulse and no sweating? This demonstrates that Wind and Cold are essentially not far apart. It is simply that Wind-pathogens are shallow while Cold-pathogens are deep. The shallow belongs to Yang, while the deep belongs to Yin. Furthermore, I have recently observed that those affected by external Cold-pathogens typically exhibit symptoms such as Cold-damage <note>original: 傷寒, Shanghan</note>, fever, a tight pulse, and an absence of perspiration. As for the specific condition of Wind-stroke, where it is said the pulse is slow and sweating occurs alongside fever, such cases are actually rare. Even when they do occur, they are less often caused by external factors and more often by internal factors. If scholars insist on using the terms "Wind" and "Cold" and the two formulas, Ma Huang Decoction and Gui Zhi Decoction, to strictly distinguish between Yin and Yang or similarities and differences, and hold stubbornly to these definitions, they will miss the mark by a wide margin. The previous volume of this section contains a differentiation between Wind and Cold which should be consulted together with this.

From this we can see that Wind and Cold are not, at root, far apart. The difference is only that the Wind pathogen is shallow and the Cold pathogen is deep: the shallow belongs to Yang and the deep belongs to Yin. Moreover, among the cases of externally contracted Cold pathogen seen in recent times, nearly all show the signs of Cold Damage <term>Shang Han</term>: fever, a tight pulse, no sweating, and so on. As for the single pattern of Wind Strike <term>Zhong Feng</term>, said to have a slow pulse with sweating and also fever, such illness is not often seen in the first place. Even when it does occur, it will seldom arise from external causes and far more often from internal causes. If students insist on using the two words "Wind" and "Cold," together with the two formulas Ephedra Decoction <term>Ma Huang Tang</term> and Cinnamon Twig Decoction <term>Gui Zhi Tang</term>, to divide Yin from Yang and sameness from difference, and cling to this as doctrine, they will stray far from the truth. In an earlier volume of this section there is a "Discussion Distinguishing Wind and Cold"; it should be examined alongside this.

There was never anyone who reached the position of Secretariat Director <note>original: 中書令 Zhongshu Ling</note>; now, considering the rank of Grand Master for Splendid Happiness <note>original: 儀同三司 Yi Tong San Si</note>, it has become a title reached through successive promotions for a Grand Councilor <note>original: 宰相 Zaixiang</note>. Under the old system, the Minister of Rites was promoted to the Ministry of Revenue; Revenue was promoted to Personnel. The Minister of Works was promoted to Justice; Justice was promoted to War. Now, the single rank of Silver Blue Grand Master for Splendid Happiness <note>original: 銀青光祿大夫 Yinqing Guanglu Dafu</note> covers all these successive ministerial promotions. 

Under the old system, a Vice Minister of Rites was promoted to Revenue; Revenue was promoted to Personnel. The Vice Minister of Works was promoted to Justice; Justice was promoted to War. Now, the single rank of Grand Master for Thorough Counsel <note>original: 正議大夫 Zhengyi Dafu</note> covers all these successive vice-ministerial promotions. 

In the past, official ranks and grades
Were difficult to advance.
Now, official ranks and grades
Are easy to elevate.

The former Ministers and attendants of the Six Ministries progressed from Rites to Revenue, and from Revenue to Personnel. Regular transfers went from Works to Justice, and from Justice to War. Now, using the single title of Silver Blue Grand Master, one covers it all. Positions that used to take twelve years to achieve are now all passed through in eight years. This is why Bi Zhongyou was deeply moved by the flaw of ranks being too easily elevated. See above for the old system regarding the appointments of Vice Ministers in the Six Oversight Departments.

There was never anyone who reached the position of Secretariat Director <note>original: 中書令 Zhongshu Ling</note>; now, considering the rank of Grand Master for Splendid Happiness <note>original: 儀同三司 Yi Tong San Si</note>, it has become a title reached through successive promotions for a Grand Councilor <note>original: 宰相 Zaixiang</note>. In a memorial, Bi Zhongyou stated: Under the old system, a Senior Deputy of the Secretariat <note>original: 平章 Pingzhang</note> would be promoted to Secretariat Director. In our dynasty, no one had ever been promoted to Secretariat Director, yet now the single rank of Grand Master for Splendid Happiness covers the successive promotions of a Grand Councilor. 

Under the old system, the Minister of Rites was promoted to the Ministry of Revenue; Revenue was promoted to Personnel. The Minister of Works was promoted to Justice; Justice was promoted to War. Now, the single rank of Silver Blue Grand Master for Splendid Happiness <note>original: 銀青光祿大夫 Yinqing Guanglu Dafu</note> covers all these successive ministerial promotions. 

Under the old system, a Vice Minister of Rites was promoted to Revenue; Revenue was promoted to Personnel. The Vice Minister of Works was promoted to Justice; Justice was promoted to War. Now, the single rank of Grand Master for Thorough Counsel <note>original: 正議大夫 Zhengyi Dafu</note> covers all these successive vice-ministerial promotions. 

In the past, official ranks and grades
Were difficult to advance.
Now, official ranks and grades
Are easy to elevate.

The former Ministers and attendants of the Six Ministries progressed from Rites to Revenue, and from Revenue to Personnel. Regular transfers went from Works to Justice, and from Justice to War. Now, using the single title of Silver Blue Grand Master, one covers it all. Positions that used to take twelve years to achieve are now all passed through in eight years. This is why Bi Zhongyou was deeply moved by the flaw of ranks being too easily elevated. See above for the old system regarding the appointments of Vice Ministers in the Six Oversight Departments.

<summary>Bi Zhongyou critiques the Song Dynasty rank reforms, arguing that consolidating multiple specific ministerial roles into single honorary titles made high-ranking promotions too easy and rapid compared to the past.</summary>

### Poetry

Let the fine rain bring a light chill once more; I sit and listen to the rustling sound as it strikes the window paper. It urges the gulls along in early spring, while the willow catkins fly feebly, sprinkling the crumbling walls. The clouds are heavy and the sky is low as the rain falls continuously; fine droplets drift down unnoticed by men. Tiny ripples rise and fill the pond.

At midnight, within the pavilions of the Five Marquises, the beauties are startled awake, grieving for the flowers. The mist dyes the purple mountains a thousand-fold emerald; it washes away all dust, leaving the six realms <note>the universe: North, South, East, West, Heaven, and Earth</note> pure. 

Du Guangting writes: The wild wind is like a hand uprooting withered trees; the surging waves are like thunder splitting broken bridges.

Xin Yu writes: Looking back at the path where the willows grew dark, clouds gradually rise over the mountains in the distance. 

Du Zirao writes: The rain startles the fish as they feed, and the old fisherman returns, holding his fishing rod as he descends the mossy bank. His home is at the ferry crossing; he departs through the dampness, the splashing sound of many droplets following his straw raincoat.

Ding Hui writes: In the middle of the night, I think of things from ten years ago; in an instant, they all come to my heart along with the rain.

Du Kehe writes: Written to celebrate the rain of a peaceful era. It has just broken through the eastern fields to the depth of the plow; it has already relieved the Emperor's <note>literally "ten thousand chariots"</note> anxious worries and should satisfy the hearts of the Three Dukes <note>high ranking officials</note> who harmonize the world. Heaven seizes the mischievous dragon and whips it until it bleeds; the thunder drives the harmonious energy, venting it as mist. On the ridges, farmers leisurely discuss the value: every inch of sweet rain is worth an inch of gold.

The Sage faces south to listen to the world and governs by turning toward the light; this principle is derived from this <note>referring to the hexagram Li, representing fire and light</note>. *Kun* is the Earth; all things are nurtured by it, therefore it is said: "They provide service in *Kun*." *Dui* represents mid-autumn; it is that which all things rejoice in, therefore it is said: "They speak of rejoicing in *Dui*." They struggle in *Qian*; *Qian* is the trigram of the northwest, referring to the contention between the <term>Yin</term> <gloss>receptive/dark principle</gloss> and <term>Yang</term> <gloss>active/light principle</gloss>. *Kan* is water; it is the trigram of the exact north, the trigram of toil; it is that to which all things return, therefore it is said: "They toil in *Kan*." *Gen* is the trigram of the northeast; it is where all things achieve their end and achieve their beginning, therefore it is said: "Achievement is spoken of in *Gen*." As for "Spirit," it is a term used to describe the wondrous functioning of all things. 

The mention of "Spirit" here clarifies that the movement, transformation, and shifting of the eight trigrams are not caused by any external force. Spirit is not a material thing; it is a term for the mystery within all things. Thus, the thunder strikes, the wind moves, the fire burns, and the water moistens.

The sages face south and listen to the affairs of the world, turning toward the light as they govern; surely they took this from the Fire trigram <note>Li</note>. The Earth trigram <note>Kun</note> is the earth. All things receive their full nourishment from it; therefore it is said, "They render service in Kun." The Lake trigram <note>Dui</note> is the height of autumn; it is where all things find their joy. Therefore it is said, "They rejoice in Dui." "They battle in Qian": Qian is the trigram of the northwest. This speaks of Yin and Yang pressing against one another. The Water trigram <note>Kan</note> is water. It is the trigram of due north, the trigram of toil, and the place to which all things return. Therefore it is said, "They toil in Kan." The Mountain trigram <note>Gen</note> is the trigram of the northeast. It is where all things complete their ending and where they complete their beginning. Therefore it is said, "They are brought to completion in Gen." The spirit <note>original: "神" shen, the divine or numinous power</note> is that which works wondrously in all things; this is what the word means.

The reason "spirit" is mentioned here is to make clear that in the movement, transformation, and succession of the Eight Trigrams, there is nothing that causes them to be so. Spirit is without form; it works wondrously in all things, and that is what the word means. Thus thunder is swift, wind moves, fire blazes, and water moistens
